case_studies.title: TokenCast: Forecasting Token Consumption During LLM Agent Execution
case_studies.abstract: When a large language model (LLM) agent executes the same task, token consumption can vary by over an order of magnitude across runs. The agent chooses its next steps based on tool feedback and intermediate results, while the growing context steadily inflates the input size of every subsequent call. The total consumption of a task is therefore hard to predict before execution and the prediction must be revised as the run unfolds. In this paper, we propose TokenCast, which learns a composable cost representation for each execution segment, recording its own consumption and the context growth it
case_studies.summary: TokenCast predicts how many tokens a large‑language‑model (LLM) agent will use during a task, helping organisations estimate costs and manage resource limits before and during execution. The authors built a system that learns a cost profile for each execution segment and updates the estimate as the agent’s context grows. The result is a more accurate token‑usage forecast, reducing surprise cost spikes for cloud‑based LLM services.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud LLM services, 1) monitor token‑usage forecasts from TokenCast to set API rate limits; 2) adjust your billing alerts based on predicted consumption; 3) use the forecast to optimise batch processing windows for cost efficiency.
case_studies.score_reasoning: TokenCast offers a practical method to forecast token usage for LLM agents, directly impacting cost management and API budgeting for IT teams. The approach is novel but within the scope of current LLM usage patterns, providing actionable insights that can be implemented in 90 days. The paper is highly relevant to IT infrastructure and operations, especially for teams managing LLM APIs and cloud billing.

case_studies.title: Tracekit: Tamper-Evident Intent-Reasoning-Action Auditing for Autonomous Coding Agents
case_studies.abstract: Autonomous coding agents read untrusted files, run shell commands and spawn sub-agents with little supervision, yet their record is usually an editable log. We present Tracekit, an open-source, dependency-free system that captures three channels for every agent session: what the human asked (intent), what the model said of its reasoning (self-report), and what it actually executed (actions). These are written to a hash-chained, externally anchorable ledger and cross-checked. Tracekit hooks into Claude Code's lifecycle events, reconstructs multi-agent hierarchies, gates tool calls with a pre-ex
case_studies.summary: Autonomous coding agents can modify files, run commands and spawn other agents without a tamper‑proof record, which makes it hard to audit their behaviour. Tracekit logs each session’s human intent, the model’s reasoning and the actual actions to a hash‑chained ledger that can be cross‑checked, giving an immutable audit trail. The system is open‑source, dependency‑free and already hooks into Claude Code’s lifecycle events.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure that uses autonomous coding agents, do the following: 1. Deploy Tracekit alongside your agents and enable its event hooks; 2. Store the resulting ledger on a secure, immutable storage (e.g. S3 with versioning or a blockchain oracle); 3. Periodically verify the hash chain against an external anchor to detect tampering.
case_studies.score_reasoning:
NOVELTY 25: Tracekit introduces a new tamper‑evident auditing framework for autonomous coding agents, a concept not previously documented in the industry.
IT_RELEVANCE 25: The system directly assists DevOps engineers, security teams, and cloud‑platform administrators in tracking and verifying the actions of AI‑driven code generators that interact with infrastructure, making it highly relevant.
VALUE_90_DAYS 19: The open‑source tool can be integrated with existing CI/CD pipelines and LLM APIs within 90 days, allowing teams to audit, flag, and mitigate risky actions, thus delivering actionable value quickly.

case_studies.title: MINT: Modeling GenAI Impact on Network Traffic
case_studies.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is becoming a mainstream network workload, yet packet-level simulators lack measure\-ment-driven GenAI traffic models. Currently researchers must approximate GenAI services using traditional sources such as file transfer and video streaming, limiting realistic network evaluation of scheduling and capacity planning. We present MINT, a measurement and modeling framework for GenAI network traffic. Using an isolated net\-work-namespace capture pipeline, we collect client-side traces from three LLM providers across four modalities, cloud and edge servers, and wired and wireles
case_studies.summary: MINT provides a data‑driven model of the packet traffic generated by generative AI workloads, fixing the gap where researchers had to fake AI traffic with unrelated services. The team built an end‑to‑end capture pipeline that logs real traffic from three large‑language‑model providers in a variety of network settings and then derives a traffic model from that data. The result is a set of validated, modality‑specific traffic profiles that can be plugged into network simulators to predict how GenAI will use bandwidth and affect scheduling.
case_studies.it_breakdown:
If you manage cloud infrastructure, here is what to do:
1. Export your existing network performance data to the MINT capture format.
2. Feed the captured traces into the MINT modelling tool to generate accurate GenAI traffic profiles.
3. Use those profiles in your capacity‑planning simulations to adjust bandwidth, QoS and routing for the expected GenAI load.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a new measurement framework for GenAI network traffic, which is a novel contribution in the context of infrastructure planning. It directly relates to network traffic management, a key concern for IT engineers, earning a moderate relevance score. However, the applicability within a 90‑day window is limited to capacity planning exercises that require setting up capture pipelines, so the actionable value is modest. The combined score exceeds 40, so the signal is considered high.

case_studies.title: Report: Progressive Disclosure of Agent Skills
case_studies.abstract: Users of Workday's deployed LLM-based agents often request features which can be addressed by defining named procedures, also known as skills, in the LLM context, effectively augmenting agents' capabilities. However, as an agent's skills library grows in size, so does the agent's operational cost. Progressive disclosure (lazy-loading) of skills as needed may reduce operational costs, but its impact on overall latency and skill-retrieval quality remains unclear. In this report, we investigate the impact empirically and find that progressive disclosure improves skill-retrieval quality but margin
case_studies.summary: The study shows that letting LLM agents load their ‘skills’ only when needed – a technique called progressive disclosure – cuts operational cost and actually improves how well the agent finds the right skill. The researchers tested this on Workday’s LLM agents and measured better skill‑retrieval quality with lower costs. This matters for anyone running large LLM workloads in the cloud.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM‑based services, adopt lazy‑loading of skill modules: 1) identify skills that can be modularised, 2) deploy a skill catalogue that loads modules on demand, and 3) monitor cost and retrieval latency to confirm savings and quality gains.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a practical technique—lazy-loading or progressive disclosure of agent skills—to reduce operational costs while improving skill‑retrieval quality in LLM‑based agents. For IT engineers and consultants managing enterprise LLM deployments (e.g., SaaS tools, API orchestration, or internal LLM solutions), this insight is novel enough to spark discussion (≈20/33). It directly addresses cost and performance concerns relevant to LLM APIs and agent orchestration, earning a high IT relevance score (≈25/33). The findings could be applied within a few weeks to tweak existing agent platforms, schedule cost‑saving measures, or advise clients, giving it a moderate but actionable value score (≈15/34).

case_studies.title: When Valid Tool Calls Change Meaning: Formation-Consistent Dispatch for LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: Tool-enabled agents form calls from model-visible interfaces, while hosts later select their implementation. Standard dispatch omits the descriptor-handler relation. An unchanged and schema-valid call can therefore acquire a different security effect during rollout, reconnect, or delayed approval. We call this failure schema-epoch drift. We present formation-consistent dispatch (FCD), which connects implementation analysis to execution authority. Reviewed profiles produce provenance-bound over-approximations of declared in-scope effects from official source. Under a closed-target approval poli
case_studies.summary: A new method called Formation‑Consistent Dispatch (FCD) stops a problem where the same tool call can later be executed with a different meaning because the system chooses a new implementation. It connects the call’s description to the authority that actually runs it, giving a proven record of what the call can do. The result is safer, predictable tool use that reduces security drift as systems evolve.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, check how your orchestration platform routes external tool calls: 1) Map each call’s descriptor to the specific implementation that will run it. 2) Ensure that the implementation’s authority matches the declared permissions in the descriptor. 3) Audit the provenance log to confirm that no unexpected changes have happened during roll‑out or reconnect. This flags a risk: if your org uses automated tool agents, verify that your dispatch logic ties calls to verified implementations.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a novel formation-consistent dispatch (FCD) technique that addresses security and consistency issues in LLM agent tool calls—a practical problem for engineers deploying LLM-driven automation. The concept of linking implementation analysis to execution authority is directly relevant to secure cloud and SaaS integration, SSO, and API gateway management. The described method can be implemented in existing agent frameworks, providing immediate actionable steps to mitigate schema-epoch drift and improve auditability in the next 90 days. Hence all three criteria score high, with a total well above 40.

case_studies.title: RSI-Router: Evolving Subtask-Level LLM Routing and Skills for Cost-Efficient Agents
case_studies.abstract: Practical deployment of large language model (LLM) agents requires strong task performance at affordable inference cost. For long-horizon agentic tasks, this performance-cost trade-off can be improved through within-task large-small model collaboration, as smaller models can handle some stages even when they cannot solve the full task. In this paper, we introduce RSI-router, a routing framework that constructs subtask-level model assignments and model-specific skills through recursive self-improvement over accumulated experience. Each iteration consists of four stages: Subtask Mining derives s
case_studies.summary: RSI‑Router solves the cost‑performance problem of running large language models (LLMs) by routing each sub‑task of a long‑horizon job to the smallest suitable model and continuously improving those routes. The authors built a recursive, self‑learning routing system that automatically assigns sub‑tasks to the right model and adds model‑specific skills as experience grows. The result is a significant drop in inference cost while keeping or improving overall task success rates.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, use RSI‑Router to optimise your LLM workloads: 1) deploy a lightweight orchestration layer that monitors model performance and cost, 2) implement sub‑task routing rules that direct simple queries to small models, 3) enable the system to auto‑update routing policies based on usage data to keep costs low.
case_studies.relevance_tag: LLM routing, cost optimization, agentic systems
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a practical framework for cost‑effective routing of sub‑tasks between large and small LLMs, offering a novel method that IT engineers could apply to optimize inference costs on cloud platforms. The routing logic directly impacts how LLM services are deployed and managed, making it highly relevant to infrastructure teams. The framework is actionable within 90 days, enabling engineers to prototype routing strategies in existing LLM‑based applications or offer cost‑saving consulting to clients.

case_studies.title: AgentWare: Automating the Lifecycle of Agentic Applications across the Edge-to-Cloud Continuum
case_studies.abstract: Deploying LLM-enabled agentic applications across the Edge-to-Cloud continuum remains challenging due to hardware heterogeneity, deployment complexity, limited observability, and the lack of systematic evaluation methods. Existing solutions address agent development, observability, or benchmarking separately, offering limited support for the full lifecycle of distributed agentic applications. This paper presents AgentWare, an AgenticOps framework that automates the provisioning, deployment, observability, and evaluation of agentic applications across Edge-to-Cloud infrastructures. AgentWare in
case_studies.summary: AgentWare is a tool that automates the full life cycle of LLM‑powered agent applications, from provisioning and deployment to observability and benchmarking, across heterogeneous edge and cloud environments. It solves the problem of manual, fragmented setup and monitoring for distributed agent systems, reducing time and complexity for operators. The result is a unified framework that speeds deployment and improves insight into performance and reliability of agent applications.
case_studies.it_breakdown:
If you manage cloud infrastructure, here is what to do:
1. Integrate AgentWare into your CI/CD pipeline to automate agent deployment on edge and cloud nodes.
2. Configure its observability modules to collect telemetry across all heterogeneous hardware.
3. Use AgentWare’s benchmarking features to evaluate agent performance and adjust resource allocation accordingly.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces AgentWare, an AgenticOps framework that automates provisioning, deployment, observability, and evaluation across edge-to-cloud infrastructures. The concept is novel for IT engineers and could be shared as a useful tool. The framework directly relates to IT operations, deployment automation, observability, and cloud management, scoring high on IT_RELEVANCE. While the framework offers potential to expedite agentic application lifecycle management, practical adoption within 90 days requires additional tooling and integration effort, so VALUE_90_DAYS is moderate. Overall, the paper scores above the 40 threshold.
